extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and graduate students in economics, political economy, and media/persuasion studies
extracted.subtask_description: A literature survey and synthesis of empirical evidence on how persuasive communication (via media, advertising, analysts, and direct contact) affects consumers, voters, donors, and investors, and on methods to measure and identify these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion rate (f)
rubrics_metrics.description: The persuasion rate f is defined as the share of listeners (or recipients) convinced by media — i.e., the fraction of exposed individuals who change their choice/behavior because of the media treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper uses persuasion rate as a central, consistent quantitative measure to compare studies (Table 1). Computation requires estimates of treatment and control action rates and exposure differences (see related metrics t_T, t_C, e_T - e_C). Use consistent definitions across studies to allow comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure rate (e_T - e_C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure rate is the difference in the fraction of individuals exposed to the persuasive message between treatment and control (e_T - e_C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate measurement of exposure is critical to compute persuasion rates. When not observed directly, authors sometimes assume e_T - e_C = 1 (e.g., mailings) or approximate exposure using diary/audience measures. Mis-measured exposure can bias persuasion estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment action rates (t_T and t_C)
rubrics_metrics.description: t_T is the share of recipients in the treatment group who take the targeted action (e.g., purchase, vote, donate); t_C is the corresponding share in the control group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the observed behavioral outcomes used with exposure measures to infer persuasion. Report sample sizes, horizons, and precise definitions of outcomes (e.g., applied for loan, turnout, vote share) so comparisons are meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for persuasion effect on vote share
rubrics_metrics.description: For vote-share outcomes the persuasion effect f can be computed from v_T, v_C, e_T - e_C and turnout terms using the expression derived in the Appendix: f = ((v_T - v_C) / (e_T - e_C)) * (t_T / (1 - v_C)), under approximations t_C = t0 and v_C = v0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Appendix gives the algebra and approximations used to account for two margins—the media inducing party-switching and inducing non-voters to turn out. Use the exact algebra when possible; report and justify approximations (e.g., tC ≈ t0). The paper illustrates application to multiple studies (DellaVigna & Kaplan, Enikolopov et al., Gerber et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer randomized and plausibly exogenous variation for causal identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should exploit randomized experiments or plausibly exogenous variation (natural experiments, instrumentation) rather than rely solely on cross-sectional correlations because advertising, coverage, and persuasion are often simultaneously determined with outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include randomized GOTV or mailer experiments, radio diffusion instrumented by signal availability (Stromberg 2004), availability of Fox News via cable (DellaVigna & Kaplan), investment bank mergers as instruments for competition (Hong & Kacperczyk), newspaper strikes reducing advertising supply (Glazer 1981), and Supreme Court decisions lifting ad bans (Milyo & Waldfogel 1999). Discuss threats to identification and use appropriate controls/instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for competition among senders as a moderator of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition among information senders (e.g., analysts, media outlets) is hypothesized to limit the scope for distortion; decreased competition may increase optimism or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical strategies include using mergers that reduce analyst competition (Hong & Kacperczyk) as instruments and comparing affected vs unaffected banks. Report effect sizes (paper reports ~10% increase in optimism bias) and test robustness across measures (forecasts, recommendations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate demand-side vs supply-side drivers of media slant
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring media political slant, distinguish whether slant arises from reader demand (preferences) or from supply-side incentives (owner preferences, advertiser pressure, reporter bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gentzkow and Shapiro measure political slant of newspapers via automated searches and estimate demand for slant vs supply of slant; control for geographic clustering of ownership to test ownership effects. Present evidence on whether newspapers choose slant to maximize circulation versus responding to owner/reporter preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for geographic clustering of ownership in ownership-effect tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing ownership effects requires controlling for the geographic clustering of ownership groups because nearby newspapers may be similar for reasons unrelated to ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gentzkow & Shapiro find that, once controlling for geographic clustering, two papers with same owner are no more politically similar than two random papers, implying small ownership effects on average. Always include such controls when testing ownership influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for advertiser influence by correlating editorial coverage with prior advertising purchases
rubrics_metrics.description: To detect advertiser-induced bias, examine whether favorable coverage is correlated with advertising expenditures by the covered firms in prior periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuter & Zitzewitz (2006) correlate mutual fund advertising space purchased in prior 12 months with subsequent favorable coverage; they find bias for some magazines but not for high-reputation outlets (NYT, WSJ). Include lagged advertising measures and compare across outlets of differing reputational capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate supply-side mechanisms via case studies of ownership and political control
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply-side incentives include owner political preferences, political pressure, and journalists’ own views; these can be tested via before/after ownership changes or when a politically connected owner gains power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Larcinese et al. (LA Times editorial shift after Otis Chandler takeover); Durante & Knight (Berlusconi’s media outlets show ownership effects in Italy). Use pre/post analysis, cross-sectional comparisons, and measures like on-air time devoted to politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report time horizon (short-term vs long-term) and emphasize long-term effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish and report the time horizon of estimated persuasion effects; many modern studies privilege short-term effects, but long-term effects may be most important for welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The survey notes only 4 of 15 studies in Table 1 examine horizons ≥1 year. Authors should design studies that measure both immediate and persistent impacts, and be explicit about horizon when reporting persuasion rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design studies to directly test theoretical models of persuasion (measure mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than only documenting reduced-form effects, studies should test model mechanisms—e.g., whether receivers account for sender incentives, how receivers seek information, or the role of credibility and uncertainty in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper identifies a gap: few studies are designed to test models directly. Collect data on receiver uncertainty, credibility signals, sender constraints, and information acquisition to permit quantitative, not just qualitative, tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish persuasion margins (switching vs turnout) when interpreting vote-share effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Media can change election outcomes by inducing voters to switch preferences or by mobilizing previously non-voters; analyses should decompose these margins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Appendix derivation of the vote-share formula explicitly accounts for both margins. When using survey-reported vote shares, report auxiliary turnout and switch estimates (t_T, v_T, v_C) and adjust calculations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instrumentation or natural experiments rather than cross-sectional correlations for advertising-price effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because advertising intensity is endogenously determined with prices and other outcomes, studies of advertising effects on prices should exploit exogenous changes in firms' ability to advertise or shocks to advertising supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Glazer (1981) uses a newspaper strike; Milyo & Waldfogel (1999) use the Supreme Court decision lifting an ad ban. Avoid relying solely on cross-sectional comparisons (Benham-style) unless careful controls and robustness checks are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and report multiple outcome domains (consumers, voters, donors, investors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion effects differ across domains; the evidence suggests communication is more effective for voters, donors, and investors than for consumers, possibly because of message crowding for consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When surveying persuasion, categorize studies by target domain, report domain-specific persuasion rates, and discuss mechanisms (e.g., personal contact matters more for voters/donors/investors). Table 1 in the paper organizes studies by domain for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate analyst conflicts of interest and affiliated analyst behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying financial analysts, compare affiliated vs unaffiliated analysts: affiliated analysts (those working for investment banks with banking transactions) tend to issue more positive recommendations and more optimistic earnings forecasts close to release dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical approaches include comparing recommendation distributions (Figure 1) and examining negative correlations between recommendations and forecasts for affiliated analysts (Malmendier & Shanthikumar). Use merger-induced changes in competition to study incentives (Hong & Kacperczyk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reputational capital as a moderating variable for editorial/advertiser bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlet reputation may limit advertiser-induced distortions: high-reputation outlets (e.g., NYT, WSJ) may show less correlation between advertiser spending and favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare outlets by reputation and test whether advertiser-coverage correlations vary. Include robustness checks for differential advertiser dependence across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document data sources, sample sizes, and time horizons when reporting persuasion estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear documentation of sample sizes (N), sample composition, years, and time horizon for effects (e.g., days, months, years) to allow interpretation and comparability (as in Table 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The survey's Table 1 reports treatment/control, context, variable, sample size, time horizon, and persuasion rate; replicate similar reporting standards in new studies for comparability and meta-analysis.
